summaries.summary: In 42 BC, Cicero raised conversational skills, stressing knowing when and what to talk about and not talking about oneself.
Conversational norms may become dynamic social conventions shaped by context, culture and language, with online practices evolving faster and little school or linguistic research.
Since Alan Turing's 1950 test, Conversational Systems have sought human-like responses, but this paper focuses on NDS improving usability and user satisfaction.
Current chatbot engines poorly handle group chats with many users and chatbots, motivating MPCS and three contributions about coordination and mediation methods and tools.
Conversation follows social conventions, and social interaction informs, contexts, creates, ratifies, refutes and ascribes power, class, gender, ethnicity and culture.
Everyday conversational conventions and patterns guide system design, with BIBREF8 distinguishing explicit interactions from implicit interactions occurring without user awareness.
Turn-by-turn social practices manage turns and subject changes, while machines struggle with context and dialogue flow, especially with multiple conversational agents.
System-initiative systems restrict options, user-initiative systems allow freedom and possible frustration, and mixed-initiative systems face interruptions, human utterances and unclear sentences.
Table TABREF5 shows system initiative in question and answer mode, Table TABREF7 shows natural dialogue with shared initiative, and another user adds challenges.
This section discusses conversational systems by types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, then presents a comparison table.
Everyday life includes many multi-user conversations, and WhatsApp and social media in the first 15 years of the 21st century expanded asynchronous text conversations.
In multiparty conversations between people and computer systems, natural language becomes a communication protocol among human users and bots.
Turn-taking chiefly distinguishes dyadic and multiparty conversations, with some social settings having explicit norms about who, when and how long participants speak.
Sacks et al. BIBREF18 found that participants generally avoid overlap and use transition-relevance places, selected-next-speaker, first starter preference, or speaker continuation.
A key challenge is determining whether context has determined the next speaker, with vocatives and a bias toward the speaker before the current.
Text message chats make transition-relevance places depend on posting, so textual chatbots must determine selected-next-speaker, with Bohus and Horowitz BIBREF19 modeling speech-based systems.
A multi-agent system (MAS) is a computational environment where software agents interact cooperatively, competitively or autonomously, forming a complex system BIBREF20.
Multi-agent coordination uses structured messages, while chatbots coordination regulates social interactions rather than lower-level synchronization, activities and information exchange.
Open multi-agent systems lack centralized control and require law-governed architecture to ensure reliable interactions according to specification and scenario.
Minsky introduced laws in 1987 BIBREF21 and Law-Governed Interaction (LGI) BIBREF22, but LGI lacks high-level social system information.
The Electronic Institution (EI) BIBREF24 supports interaction norms through high-level abstractions including agent roles, norms and scenes.
XMLaw and the M-Law framework BIBREF25 BIBREF26 enforce laws through norms and clocks, intercepting messages and applying permissions, prohibitions and obligations.
Conversational systems have mainly three architectures: totally rule-oriented, totally data-oriented, and a mix of rules and data-oriented.
Data-oriented architectures learn models from dialogue samples using machine learning or extracted rules instead of explicitly defined rules.
BIBREF33 surveys public corpora classified by data, interaction and domain, including Switchboard dataset and Dialog State Tracking Challenge (DSTC) tasks.
By types of intentions, conversational systems are classified as goal-driven or task oriented, and non-goal-driven or end-to-end systems.
CognIA's interaction norms are implicit, not obligations, permissions and prohibitions, because the goal was evaluating overall architecture with a small norm set.
Current chatbot engines poorly handle group chats with many users and chatbots, motivating MPCS and three main contributions rather than advancing MPCS norms.

System-initiative systems restrict user options with direct questions, user-initiative systems risk frustration, and mixed-initiative dialogue faces interruptions, human utterances, and unclear sentences.
Table TABREF5 shows system-initiative question and answer dialogue, Table TABREF7 shows natural mixed-initiative dialogue, and adding another user creates other challenges.
In Table TABREF12, S1 does not reply to user-only utterances, later invites expert systems, and S3 alone replies about the certificate option.
Table TABREF12 illustrates that chatbots need contextual knowledge of when to reply, and MPCS has four dimensions of understanding and replying.
A.L.I.C.E. appeared in 1995, uses AIML, has more than 40,000 categories versus ELIZA's about 200, and cannot pass the Turing test.
Early 2010s advances enabled text-based chatbots and spoken interfaces, but deployments were mostly dyadic, yielding two interaction types based on chat membership.
A Dyadic Chatbot always handles received utterances, works with two members or name mentions, lacks coordination, and includes ELIZA through modern state-of-the-art systems.
Multiparty chatbot creation combines chatbot research and multi-agent coordination research, but lacks multiparty-aware or governed chatbots that could increase system trust.
Multi-agent coordination uses structured formalized messages, while chatbot coordination regulates social interactions rather than lower-level synchronization, activities, and information exchange.
The paragraph states the topic: Coordinated Aware Chatbots in a Multiparty Conversation.
Chatbot engines lack research on coordination laws integrated with natural language, and the proposed architecture is claimed first for coordinated aware multiparty chatbots.
Rule-oriented architectures provide manually coded replies, include Eliza and Parry, and may use grammars, mappings, propositional logic, or FOL with Objects, Relations, and Functions.
Prolog FOL specifications and facts form a rule-oriented chatbot knowledge base, while OntBot maps ontologies to relational databases but faces difficult data retrieval interfaces.
Rule-oriented chatbot intelligence depends on knowledge base size and quality, and good knowledge bases may require years to create depending on the domain.
Data-oriented systems may use information retrieval, neural networks, HMM, and POMDP, with examples Cleverbot and Tay, plus Microsoft's RCNN-based unified multi-turn multi-task SLU approach.
Current A.L.I.C.E. uses incremental or interactive learning where a person monitors conversations, creates AIML content, and receives automatically detected new input patterns.
Goal-driven systems execute application-specific back-end tasks, commonly use POMDP, HMM, and Memory Networks, and face annotated corpora collection, domain transfer, and scaling issues.
Non-goal-driven systems generate utterances from user input, use RNN, Dynamic Context-Sensitive Generation, Memory Networks, and HTMM, and can simulate users for goal-driven systems.
Dialogue systems may support context reasoning, needed for partial information over turns, and BIBREF38 identifies context-level errors among the top-10 confusing errors.
Most context reasoning approaches use rules, logics, and knowledge bases, encoding dialogue facts in FOL statements to query an inference engine, as in Table TABREF37.
A rule-oriented chatbot can use Rya or any triple store and call the semantic search engine to inference and generate proper answers.
Recent papers use neural networks to predict the next utterance in non-goal-driven systems considering context, including Memory Networks BIBREF40 and work BIBREF36.
Sukhbaatar's model encodes word order and temporal context, supports back propagation through memory accesses, but is untested for goal-oriented systems and multi-party bots.
Current conversational system platforms fall into plugging, creating, and service chatbot categories, summarized in Table TABREF43, but lack coordinated multiparty governance or mediation support.
The hybrid rule and machine learning-based MPCS architecture defines chatbot knowledge with Chat Group, Members, Roles, and Chatbot as a Role.
Members send Utterances classified by Intent with Speech Act, while Intent Flow triggers Chatbot Actions that produce Utterances and maps answer intentions as directed graph G.
Each intent's class may refer to many Entities, which in turn may be associated with several Features.
Figure FIGREF48 shows the workflow from utterance to reply, with a Hub broadcasting messages and norms as prohibition, obligation, or permission.
After broadcast, Parsing uses a Topic Classifier, Dependency Parsing, metadata extraction, Frame parsing, Context storage, Intent Classifier, Speech Act retrieval, and Event Detector.
The domain-dependent topic classifier is optional but helps the chatbot react earlier when intent, action, topic, or behavior is missing or misunderstood.
Frame-based parsing uses dependency trees and rules to fill slots with extracted values, representing fields as Entities and Features and prompting for missing investment information.
One listed task is the creation of dataset of intents to train the classification algorithm.
Another listed task is the creation of dataset of trees of intents, the same as defined in i), which maps the goals.
Training sets for dialogues can use incremental Wizard of Oz collection, manual intent classification, first-version training, and expansion in classes and samples.
The Speech Act Classifier can use dictionaries or machine learning, with more classes increasing flexibility, and the table presents main general speech act classes BIBREF43.
There are at least as many Action classes as Speech Act classes, and domain-specific classes like "Inform_News" or "Inform_Factoids" enhance chatbot answering.
This component implements Action class behavior, with shared basic behaviors for greetings, thanks, or not understood, and domain-dependent implementations for informing, querying, or proposing.
Figure FIGREF59 shows the generic workflow where task-oriented actions execute tasks, may access external Internet services, generate replies, and finish when no more tasks are needed.
For chatbot coordination, one or more mediator chatbots may invite chatbots to the chat group and redirect utterances at this step.
The Filtering phase solves who should reply to the utterance and may be enforced by the Hub.
This section presents an implementation of the conceptual architecture, the SABIA framework, the CognIA application, and accuracy and automated tests.
SABIA implements Members as Akka UntypedActor Actors, uses singleton SabiaActorSystem and parsers, and manages chat groups through Chat Group behavior.
SABIA initializes a singleton dependency parsing service URL and uses tagUtterance on each utterance arrival, parsing the returned JSON dependency tree with depth-first search.
CognIA instantiates Sabia with group chats containing multiple users and chatbots, including a mediator for financial matters and investment options.
Table TABREF71 uses mixed-initiative dialogue and a dialogue mediator, with intentions including Q&A, investment simulations, and subjective opinions.
Table SECREF72 presents CognIA interaction norms, with Trigger, Pre-Conditions, and Behavior columns, including CDB, Savings Account, Query_Calculation, cdbguru, and poupancaguru.
CognIA's interaction norms are implicit from behavior, not explicitly obligations, permissions, or prohibitions, and the small Table SECREF72 set required no model checking or conflict verification.
On group chat creation, Cognia chatbot is available, joins with the mediator role, and the user joins with the owner_user role.
On utterance sent, if an utterance mentions a chatbot but has no other text, the chatbot replies "How can I help you?"
Dependency parsing is crucial for computing return of investment; CognIA replaced fragile regular expressions with a TensorFlow SyntaxNet model for Portuguese.
Given the dependency tree, frame parsing extracts entities and features into context, then replaces them with reserved characters.
CognIA adds action-specific speech act classes, using Query_Calculation for computation requests and Inform_Calculation for replies, listed in Table TABREF81.
With no public Portuguese financial intents dataset, CognIA used Wizard of Oz to collect 124 questions and built 37 intent classes with 415 samples, ranging from 3 to 37 per class.
CognIA first used a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier for easy retraining, then employed Support Vector Machines with a Gaussian kernel and grid-search optimized parameters.
Intent classes were manually mapped to action classes and dependent entities and features, with Table TABREF85 summarizing intent classes per action class in CognIA.
Most action classes used SABIA's default behavior, such as Greet and Bye implemented using rapport.
Search News, Compute, and Ask More are the classes requiring specific implementation for CognIA.
Ask More has the mediator request missing investment return variables before redirecting queries, checking context against intent flow dependencies manually added to the database.

SABIA's validation framework provides a high-level language for integration test scenarios, simulates users, collects response time and resource metrics, and requires automatic tests before deployment.
Testers provide dialogues as ordered sets of user utterances and expected chatbot response pairs, with Table UID98 showing a typical CognIA dialogue.
The framework supports concurrent simulated users, checks expected responses within a maximum time, collects response times and resource metrics, and is divided into SABIA-side and client-side parts.
The tests provide CognIA sanity checks and SABIA performance analysis, validating correct answers, reasonable time, resource consumption, network bandwidth, CPU, and memory.
CognIA was deployed on IBM Bluemix with specified server resources, two 10-utterance dialogues were built, and tests were repeated until standard deviation was less than 1%.
Test 1 ran both dialogues for one user with a 30 seconds maximum wait, and Mediator, CDBExpert, and SavingsAccountExpert gave all expected responses.
Figure FIGREF101 shows response times for dialogue INLINEFORM0, with CDBExpert answering "what is cdb?", Mediator taking longest, and response 19 reaching 20 seconds.
Test 2 ran dialogue INLINEFORM0 with eight concurrent simulated users, a 240 seconds maximum wait, and Figure FIGREF102 shows median response times with maximum and minimum markers.

AIML language allows:
Symbolic reduction reduces complex grammatical forms to simpler ones.
Divide and conquer splits an input into two or more subparts and combines the responses to each.
Synonyms map different ways of saying the same thing to the same reply.
Detecting keywords anywhere in the input act like triggers for a reply.
Conditionals are certain forms of branching to produce a reply.
Any combination of (1)-(6) is allowed.
U: My husband would like to invest with me.
S: Who else in your family would like to invest with you?
Excess/lack of proposition means the utterance provides no new proposition or excessive information than required.
Contradiction means the utterance contains propositions contradicting what the system or user said.
Non-relevant topic means the utterance topic is irrelevant to the current context.
Unclear relation means the utterance's relation to the current topic is unclear.
Topic switch error means the system missed the user's topic switch and continued the previous topic.

The proposed architecture addresses the challenges as the following:
What is the message/utterance about? solved by the Parsing phase;
Who should reply to the utterance? solved by the Filtering phase and may be enforced by the Hub;
How the reply should be built/generated? solved by the Acting phase;
When should the reply be sent? may be solved by the Acting phase or the Filtering phase, and may be enforced by the Hub;
And Context and Logging module is used throughout all phases.

Dialogue systems may support context reasoning, needed for partial information over turns, and BIBREF38 identifies context-level errors among the top-10 confusing errors.
Most context reasoning approaches use rules, logics, and knowledge bases, encoding dialogue facts in FOL statements to query an inference engine, as in Table TABREF37.
A rule-oriented chatbot can use Rya or any triple store and call the semantic search engine to inference and generate proper answers.
Recent papers use neural networks to predict the next utterance in non-goal-driven systems considering context, including Memory Networks BIBREF40 and work BIBREF36.
Sukhbaatar's model encodes word order and temporal context, supports back propagation through memory accesses, but is untested for goal-oriented systems and multi-party bots.
Current conversational system platforms fall into plugging, creating, and service chatbot categories, summarized in Table TABREF43, but lack coordinated multiparty governance or mediation support.
The hybrid rule and machine learning-based MPCS architecture defines chatbot knowledge with Chat Group, Members, Roles, and Chatbot as a Role.
Members send Utterances classified by Intent with Speech Act, while Intent Flow triggers Chatbot Actions that produce Utterances and maps answer intentions as directed graph G.
Each intent's class may refer to many Entities, which in turn may be associated with several Features.
Figure FIGREF48 shows the workflow from utterance to reply, with a Hub broadcasting messages and norms as prohibition, obligation, or permission.
After broadcast, Parsing uses a Topic Classifier, Dependency Parsing, metadata extraction, Frame parsing, Context storage, Intent Classifier, Speech Act retrieval, and Event Detector.
The domain-dependent topic classifier is optional but helps the chatbot react earlier when intent, action, topic, or behavior is missing or misunderstood.
Frame-based parsing uses dependency trees and rules to fill slots with extracted values, representing fields as Entities and Features and prompting for missing investment information.
One listed task is the creation of dataset of intents to train the classification algorithm.
Another listed task is the creation of dataset of trees of intents, the same as defined in i), which maps the goals.
Training sets for dialogues can use incremental Wizard of Oz collection, manual intent classification, first-version training, and expansion in classes and samples.
The Speech Act Classifier can use dictionaries or machine learning, with more classes increasing flexibility, and the table presents main general speech act classes BIBREF43.
There are at least as many Action classes as Speech Act classes, and domain-specific classes like "Inform_News" or "Inform_Factoids" enhance chatbot answering.
This component implements Action class behavior, with shared basic behaviors for greetings, thanks, or not understood, and domain-dependent implementations for informing, querying, or proposing.
Figure FIGREF59 shows the generic workflow where task-oriented actions execute tasks, may access external Internet services, generate replies, and finish when no more tasks are needed.
For chatbot coordination, one or more mediator chatbots may invite chatbots to the chat group and redirect utterances at this step.
The Filtering phase solves who should reply to the utterance and may be enforced by the Hub.
This section presents an implementation of the conceptual architecture, the SABIA framework, the CognIA application, and accuracy and automated tests.
SABIA implements Members as Akka UntypedActor Actors, uses singleton SabiaActorSystem and parsers, and manages chat groups through Chat Group behavior.
SABIA initializes a singleton dependency parsing service URL and uses tagUtterance on each utterance arrival, parsing the returned JSON dependency tree with depth-first search.
CognIA instantiates Sabia with group chats containing multiple users and chatbots, including a mediator for financial matters and investment options.
Table TABREF71 uses mixed-initiative dialogue and a dialogue mediator, with intentions including Q&A, investment simulations, and subjective opinions.
Table SECREF72 presents CognIA interaction norms, with Trigger, Pre-Conditions, and Behavior columns, including CDB, Savings Account, Query_Calculation, cdbguru, and poupancaguru.
CognIA's interaction norms are implicit from behavior, not explicitly obligations, permissions, or prohibitions, and the small Table SECREF72 set required no model checking or conflict verification.
On group chat creation, Cognia chatbot is available, joins with the mediator role, and the user joins with the owner_user role.
On utterance sent, if an utterance mentions a chatbot but has no other text, the chatbot replies "How can I help you?"
Dependency parsing is crucial for computing return of investment; CognIA replaced fragile regular expressions with a TensorFlow SyntaxNet model for Portuguese.
Given the dependency tree, frame parsing extracts entities and features into context, then replaces them with reserved characters.
CognIA adds action-specific speech act classes, using Query_Calculation for computation requests and Inform_Calculation for replies, listed in Table TABREF81.
With no public Portuguese financial intents dataset, CognIA used Wizard of Oz to collect 124 questions and built 37 intent classes with 415 samples, ranging from 3 to 37 per class.
CognIA first used a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier for easy retraining, then employed Support Vector Machines with a Gaussian kernel and grid-search optimized parameters.
Intent classes were manually mapped to action classes and dependent entities and features, with Table TABREF85 summarizing intent classes per action class in CognIA.
Most action classes used SABIA's default behavior, such as Greet and Bye implemented using rapport.
Search News, Compute, and Ask More are the classes requiring specific implementation for CognIA.
Ask More has the mediator request missing investment return variables before redirecting queries, checking context against intent flow dependencies manually added to the database.

SABIA's validation framework provides a high-level language for integration test scenarios, simulates users, collects response time and resource metrics, and requires automatic tests before deployment.
Testers provide dialogues as ordered sets of user utterances and expected chatbot response pairs, with Table UID98 showing a typical CognIA dialogue.
The framework supports concurrent simulated users, checks expected responses within a maximum time, collects response times and resource metrics, and is divided into SABIA-side and client-side parts.
The tests provide CognIA sanity checks and SABIA performance analysis, validating correct answers, reasonable time, resource consumption, network bandwidth, CPU, and memory.
CognIA was deployed on IBM Bluemix with specified server resources, two 10-utterance dialogues were built, and tests were repeated until standard deviation was less than 1%.
Test 1 ran both dialogues for one user with a 30 seconds maximum wait, and Mediator, CDBExpert, and SavingsAccountExpert gave all expected responses.
Figure FIGREF101 shows response times for dialogue INLINEFORM0, with CDBExpert answering "what is cdb?", Mediator taking longest, and response 19 reaching 20 seconds.
Test 2 ran dialogue INLINEFORM0 with eight concurrent simulated users, a 240 seconds maximum wait, and Figure FIGREF102 shows median response times with maximum and minimum markers.

The proposed architecture addresses the challenges as the following:
What is the message/utterance about? solved by the Parsing phase;
Who should reply to the utterance? solved by the Filtering phase and may be enforced by the Hub;
How the reply should be built/generated? solved by the Acting phase;
When should the reply be sent? may be solved by the Acting phase or the Filtering phase, and may be enforced by the Hub;
And Context and Logging module is used throughout all phases.
